Natural selection doesn't really work in the way you're describing since in many cases we're accelerating the pace so much that nature has no chance to adapt. Taken to extreme we could just nuke an animals habitat and everything whose primary residence there would likely go extinct in short order regardless of how otherwise adaptive they would have been.

But a more practical example is stuff like logging and damming. When we change animals' habitats in this way it tends to happen extremely rapidly. It may not even be something that directly effects the animals but for instance we destroy a certain type of plant edible than a smaller animal primarily ate and that animal in turn fed larger predators. Suddenly we're ripping up the entire food chain from the bottom up. If this process happened gradually with a steady decline of that food source then I agree that evolution would probably kick in and we'd see adaptive measures take place as populations and diets adjusted, but when you go from 100 to 0 in a matter of a century or two, and in some cases far faster, then there no real time for any sort of natural adaptation.
